# Technical brief: presenting from your own device with a native app, watched live in a web page

**Bottom line:** The browser-native path is `navigator.mediaDevices.getDisplayMedia()` (Screen Capture API) on the presenter's device, optionally refined by Region/Element Capture, then delivery via WebRTC. For 1 presenter + ~10 viewers, an SFU is the right delivery architecture; a mesh works but is already past its comfortable range. A presenter-side extension or companion app is an optional upgrade that trades install friction for a quieter permission flow and more deterministic capture (tab audio, no re-prompt per session, offscreen/background operation).

---

## 1. getDisplayMedia / Screen Capture API

### What can be captured

The W3C Screen Capture spec defines three **display surface** types — `monitor` (a physical display or group of displays), `window` (a single application window), and `browser` (a tab/browsing context) — collected in the `DisplayCaptureSurfaceType` enum ([Screen Capture WD, §4 Terminology and §5.4.15](https://www.w3.org/TR/screen-capture/#dom-displaycapturesurfacetype)). MDN summarizes: "Sharing surfaces include the contents of a browser tab, a complete window, and a monitor" ([MDN: Using the Screen Capture API – visible vs. logical display surfaces](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Screen_Capture_API/Using_Screen_Capture#visible_vs._logical_display_surfaces)).

`getDisplayMedia()` returns a `MediaStream` with exactly one video track and at most one audio track ([MDN: getDisplayMedia() – Return value](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaDevices/getDisplayMedia#return_value); [Screen Capture WD §5.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/screen-capture/#dom-mediadevices-getdisplaymedia)). Video-only capture is the norm; `video: false` is a `TypeError`; audio-only requests must be rejected ([Screen Capture WD §5.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/screen-capture/#dom-mediadevices-getdisplaymedia)).

Relevant for a presenter: a minimized/occluded window continues to be captured as a **logical display surface**, but a window that closes ends its track, and a minimized source may mute it ([Screen Capture WD §5.2 Closed and Minimized Display Surfaces](https://www.w3.org/TR/screen-capture/#hidden-display-surfaces)). Capture of a monitor vs. window vs. tab is user-chosen; the `displaySurface` constraint may only *preselect* a pane in the picker, never restrict the user's choice ([Screen Capture WD §5.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/screen-capture/#dom-mediadevices-getdisplaymedia); [Chrome: Privacy-preserving screen sharing controls – displaySurface](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/screen-sharing-controls#displaySurface)).

### Audio capture, per browser (this is where the differences are)

The spec is deliberately permissive: "the user agent is allowed not to return audio even if the audio constraint is present," and audio sources "may be a particular window, browser, the entire system audio or any combination thereof" ([Screen Capture WD §5.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/screen-capture/#dom-mediadevices-getdisplaymedia)). MDN likewise: audio is optional and the returned stream "may still have only one video track, with no audio" ([MDN: Using the Screen Capture API – Capturing shared audio](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Screen_Capture_API/Using_Screen_Capture#capturing_shared_audio)).

Per-browser reality (from the MDN browser-compat-data source that feeds the MDN compat table, [`api/MediaDevices.json` → `getDisplayMedia.audio_capture_support`](https://github.com/mdn/browser-compat-data/blob/main/api/MediaDevices.json)):

| Browser | Audio capture | Notes (verbatim from BCD) |
|---|---|---|
| Chrome | ✅ since 74 | "On **Windows** and ChromeOS, the entire system audio can be captured when sharing an entire screen. On Linux and macOS, only the audio of a tab can be captured." |
| Edge | ✅ (mirrors Chrome) | same as Chrome |
| Firefox | ❌ | `version_added: false` — no display-capture audio support |
| Safari | ❌ | `version_added: false` — no display-capture audio support |

**Windows (Chrome/Edge) specifics:** when the presenter shares an entire screen, Chrome offers "Share system audio" (the whole machine's audio — i.e., a PowerPoint video's sound plays through); when sharing a tab, Chrome offers "Share tab audio". Chrome's documentation confirms both: "Sharing tab audio is offered in 'Chrome Tab' pane, but not in 'Entire Screen' pane," and the `systemAudio: "exclude"` option removes the system-audio checkbox when sharing screens ([Chrome: screen-sharing-controls – systemAudio](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/screen-sharing-controls#systemAudio)). Option availability in Chrome/Edge: `systemAudio` since Chrome 105 (default `include`), `windowAudio` since Chrome 141 (only `exclude`/`system` values supported, not `window`; Edge had a 141–143 default quirk), `monitorTypeSurfaces` since 119 (default `include`), `surfaceSwitching` since 107 (default `exclude`), `selfBrowserSurface` since 107 (default flipped to `exclude` in 112), `controller` (CaptureController) since 109 ([BCD `getDisplayMedia` subfeatures](https://github.com/mdn/browser-compat-data/blob/main/api/MediaDevices.json)). Note: none of these sources differentiate Windows 10 vs. Windows 11 — the documented behavior is "Windows," not a specific OS build, so plan for the same API behavior on both. `windowAudio` is the option to watch: it hints whether window-sharing offers window-only audio, system audio, or none ([MDN: getDisplayMedia – windowAudio](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaDevices/getDisplayMedia#windowaudio); the spec enum is `WindowAudioPreferenceEnum`, [Screen Capture WD §5.4.6](https://www.w3.org/TR/screen-capture/#dom-windowaudiopreferenceenum)).

### Permission model

- The user must be prompted **every session** — a `"granted"` display-capture permission can never be persisted; the permission state is only ever `prompt` or `denied` ([Screen Capture WD §6 Permissions Integration](https://www.w3.org/TR/screen-capture/#permissions-intergration)).
- Transient user activation is required, the document must be focused, and constraints cannot narrow the source list presented to the user ([MDN: getDisplayMedia – Security](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaDevices/getDisplayMedia#security)).
- `Permissions-Policy: display-capture=(self)` (default allowlist `self`) governs embedding in iframes ([Screen Capture WD §7](https://www.w3.org/TR/screen-capture/#feature-policy-integration); [MDN Using Screen Capture – Security](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Screen_Capture_API/Using_Screen_Capture#security)).
- Browsers must show a privacy indicator during capture; display sources are not enumerable via `enumerateDevices()`; the capture prompt itself must not appear in the captured stream ([Screen Capture WD §8, §5.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/screen-capture/#privacy-indicator-requirements); [MDN Using Screen Capture](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Screen_Capture_API/Using_Screen_Capture#options_and_constraints)).

---

## 2. Element Capture and Region Capture — status

These matter for your use case: a presenter who shares the browser tab containing the app can crop the stream to just the slide area, excluding speaker notes and UI.

**Region Capture** — **W3C First Public Working Draft, 12 July 2023** ([Region Capture spec](https://www.w3.org/TR/mediacapture-region/)); shipped in Chrome/Edge **104+, desktop only** ([Chrome: Better tab sharing with Region Capture](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/region-capture)). Mechanics: `CropTarget.fromElement(el)` produces a serializable handle; `track.cropTo(cropTarget)` (on `BrowserCaptureMediaStreamTrack`) crops every frame to the element's bounding box, tracking layout changes automatically ([spec §6.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/mediacapture-region/#browsercapturemediastreamtrack); [MDN: Using the Element Capture and Region Capture APIs](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Screen_Capture_API/Element_Region_Capture#the_region_capture_api)). Caveats: it is **cropping, not compositing** — occluding content (dropdowns, notifications) appears in the capture; if the target scrolls out of view, no frames are produced until it's visible again ([spec §6.2.2.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/mediacapture-region/#empty-crop-target)). It works on tab capture (self-capture recommended); Chrome draws its "captured tab" blue border around the cropped region. The spec also notes `getViewportMedia` — a capture API tailored for this — "is still unspecified and unimplemented" ([spec §3.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/mediacapture-region/#practical-use-case)).

**Element Capture** — **not yet a W3C TR**; the specification lives at [screen-share.github.io/element-capture](https://screen-share.github.io/element-capture/) (community incubation), documented by Chrome ([Capture a video stream from any element](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/element-capture)) and MDN ([RestrictionTarget](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/RestrictionTarget), [BrowserCaptureMediaStreamTrack.restrictTo()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/BrowserCaptureMediaStreamTrack/restrictTo)). Shipped in Chrome/Edge **132+, desktop only** ("Element Capture is available from Chrome 132 on desktop only"). Mechanics: `RestrictionTarget.fromElement(el)` + `track.restrictTo(target)`; unlike Region Capture it captures the DOM subtree itself, removing both occluding and occluded content — the better fit for "share only the slide, never my chat overlay." Constraints: the element must form a stacking context (`isolation: isolate`), frames stop if the element becomes ineligible (`display:none`, etc.), it is currently restricted to self-capture, and captured frames carry no alpha channel ([Chrome: element-capture](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/element-capture)).

---

## 3. Delivering the stream to ~10 concurrent viewers: mesh vs. SFU

**Mesh (P2P).** Each participant maintains a peer connection to every other participant. The presenter therefore **uploads one encoded copy of the presentation stream per viewer**. LiveKit's SFU documentation puts the practical ceiling plainly: "This works well for a set of **2-3 peers**, but how many people have an internet connection which can consistently upload **five 720p (1.5Mbps) video streams** simultaneously? Not many. Thus, scaling WebRTC to groups of more than 2-3 people requires a client-server model" ([LiveKit: LiveKit SFU – P2P vs. MCU vs. SFU](https://docs.livekit.io/reference/internals/livekit-sfu.md)). For your topology — 1 presenter + 10 viewers, and viewers with cameras/mics also publishing — the presenter would upload 10 simultaneous streams (≈15 Mbps at 720p, plus 10× the encode work), and every viewer would decode 10 incoming streams. A mesh is workable for small groups (roughly up to 4–6 total participants in practice), but **at ~10 viewers it is already past the point where the SFU is the appropriate choice**; the deciding factors are presenter uplink bandwidth (N−1 × bitrate) and per-client decode load, both of which grow linearly with N.

**SFU (Selective Forwarding Unit).** All three servers you named are SFUs; each forwards one upstream copy to many downstream viewers without decoding or re-encoding:

- **mediasoup** — a Node.js library; "A router behaves as an **SFU** (Selective Forwarding Unit): it forwards RTP packets between producers and consumers … however it does neither decode nor transcode media packets" ([mediasoup docs – Scalability](https://mediasoup.org/documentation/v3/scalability/)). Capacity guidance: one worker (one CPU core) "can typically handle over ~500 consumers in total"; a 4-peer room consumes 24 consumers; for 1-to-many, one router is comfortable "up to 200-300 viewers (400-600 consumers)," beyond which you fan out via `router.pipeToRouter()` and server-side re-encoders ([mediasoup – Scalability](https://mediasoup.org/documentation/v3/scalability/)). Ten viewers is ~10–20 consumers — trivially inside a single worker's envelope.
- **LiveKit** — "an opinionated, horizontally-scaling WebRTC Selective Forwarding Unit"; publisher sends once, server "forwards a copy of each stream … to each interested subscriber without manipulating any underlying packets," with automatic per-subscriber bitrate adaptation ([LiveKit: LiveKit SFU](https://docs.livekit.io/reference/internals/livekit-sfu.md)). LiveKit also has first-class screen-share publishing in its SDKs (`setScreenShareEnabled`, `createScreenTracks({audio:true})`, with a browser-support caveat pointing at the MDN table) ([LiveKit: Screen sharing](https://docs.livekit.io/transport/media/screenshare.md)).
- **Janus** — "a general purpose WebRTC server … relaying RTP/RTCP and messages"; no transcoding in the core ("Janus is a simple intermediary … it doesn't provide any transcoding functionality per-se"), videoconferencing via the VideoRoom plugin, and scaling by "implementing a wrapper/controller application that is in charge of multiple Janus instances" distributing load ([Janus docs](https://janus.conf.meetecho.com/docs/), [Janus FAQ – transcoding](https://janus.conf.meetecho.com/docs/FAQ.html#transcoding), [Janus FAQ – scaling](https://janus.conf.meetecho.com/docs/FAQ.html#scaling)).

For 10 viewers, all three handle the load with enormous headroom; the choice is operational (self-host vs. managed, signaling effort, recording/transcription needs), not capacity. Only if you insist on zero server infrastructure would a mesh work at this size — at the cost of the presenter's uplink and CPU.

---

## 4. Latency expectations

No standard mandates millisecond numbers, so treat these as typical ranges: the architectural facts are cited, the ranges are engineering judgment.

- **WebRTC itself** is designed for interactive real-time use ("add real-time communication capabilities … video, voice, and generic data to be sent between peers" — [webrtc.org](https://webrtc.org/)); end-to-end ("glass-to-glass") latency for an interactive WebRTC session is generally in the ~100–500 ms range depending on network and jitter buffering.
- **Mesh:** one media leg (presenter → viewer) plus capture/encode on the presenter and decode/render on the viewer. No extra relay hop, so it is the lowest-latency option, all else equal.
- **SFU:** two media legs (presenter → SFU → viewer). Because an SFU forwards RTP packets without transcoding — "low-latency, high-bandwidth media forwarding … without manipulating any underlying packets" (LiveKit); "forwards RTP packets … neither decode nor transcode" (mediasoup); "simple intermediary" with no transcoding (Janus) — the added latency is roughly one extra network traversal plus SFU-side buffering/queuing, typically on the order of tens of milliseconds (I'd budget ~50–100 ms over mesh in practice). This is why screen-sharing products universally use SFUs rather than MCUs; an MCU that decodes/composites/re-encodes would add meaningfully more delay.
- **Extension/native companion capture:** delivery latency is identical (still WebRTC); the capture-side difference is usually negligible (browser capture adds one composition hop). The real difference is *reliability* of the capture path, not latency.

---

## 5. Presenter-side companion app or browser extension — what it buys over getDisplayMedia

Two flavors, both documented:

**Browser extension.** Two relevant APIs:
- `chrome.tabCapture` — grants the extension a `MediaStream` of a specific tab's video **and audio** with the `tabCapture` permission, no per-session picker: "It can only be called after the user invokes an extension, such as by clicking the extension's action button … Capture is maintained across page navigations within the tab, and stops when the tab is closed." Tab audio is included (and suppressed from local speakers unless you route it back through an `AudioContext` — the same effect as `suppressLocalAudioPlayback`). Stream IDs can be handed to an offscreen document (Chrome 116+) ([chrome.tabCapture reference](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/reference/api/tabCapture)).
- `chrome.desktopCapture` — `chooseDesktopMedia()` shows the screen/window/tab picker once (per request), returns an opaque `streamId` you pass to `getUserMedia()` with `chromeMediaSource` constraints; the callback's `canRequestAudioTrack` tells you whether the user left "Share audio" checked, and `audio` is a selectable source type ([chrome.desktopCapture reference](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/reference/api/desktopCapture)).

**What an extension buys over a plain web page:** (1) a deterministic, pre-authorized capture target — you know exactly which tab/window is being captured, and `tabCapture` keeps capturing that tab even as the presenter switches tabs (a plain `getDisplayMedia` stream switches to whatever surface the user picked and can be redirected only via the browser's own "share this tab instead" control, `surfaceSwitching`, [Chrome screen-sharing-controls](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/screen-sharing-controls#surfaceSwitching)); (2) tab audio with no system-audio ambiguity; (3) a one-time install permission instead of a per-session prompt; (4) the ability to run capture in an offscreen/background document so the presenting UI can be clean. Cost: the user must install and trust an extension, and extensions cannot capture arbitrary application windows without the picker (`desktopCapture` still shows the chooser).

**Native companion app (e.g., Windows).** An installed helper can capture *any* OS window (PowerPoint's window, not just browser surfaces) via OS-level capture APIs (e.g., Windows.Graphics.Capture/Desktop Duplication), mix system audio at the OS level, and then publish to your server either through a WebRTC stack embedded in the app or by streaming to your SFU via WHIP/WHEP-style ingestion (Janus documents WHIP ingestion as a first-class broadcasting path, [Janus FAQ – WHIP](https://janus.conf.meetecho.com/docs/FAQ.html#videos); LiveKit's Ingress service exists precisely to "bring live streams from non-WebRTC sources into LiveKit rooms," [LiveKit Ingress](https://docs.livekit.io/transport/media/ingress-egress/ingress.md)). What this buys over `getDisplayMedia`: no browser permission UI at all, reliable window targeting (the PowerPoint window stays captured regardless of focus/occlusion), richer audio control, and full control of encoding. Cost: install/update/maintenance burden, platform-specific code, and a trust decision — and per the Screen Capture spec's "elevated permissions" guidance, OS-level capture is exactly the class of capability that warrants a deliberate, install-like consent process ([Screen Capture WD §9.2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/screen-capture/#elevated-permissions)).

**Recommendation for your case:** if the "own native application" is a *browser-based* presenter, `getDisplayMedia` + Region/Element Capture + an SFU (any of the three) is sufficient and zero-install; add an extension only if the per-session picker or tab-audio handling becomes a problem. If the presenter must share a true native app window (PowerPoint), the browser extension's `desktopCapture` is the middle ground, and a companion app is the most robust option — at the price of shipping and maintaining native code.

---

### Remaining uncertainty

- **Windows 11 specifically:** all cited sources say "Windows," not "Windows 11"; I found no documented Chrome/Edge behavior that differs between Windows 10 and 11 for this API. Treat the system-audio-on-screen-share behavior as OS-version-independent.
- **Element Capture:** the spec is an incubator draft (screen-share.github.io), not a W3C TR, and `restrictTo()` is currently self-capture-only — fine for a presenter sharing their own tab, but unusable for capturing *other* tabs until that restriction lifts.
- **Latency numbers:** the sub-second ranges are typical-practice figures, not spec-mandated; the only hard, cited facts are that SFUs forward without transcoding and that mesh's P2P scaling collapses beyond ~2–3 publishers (LiveKit's own wording). If you need guaranteed numbers, plan a measurement pass with your actual network.
- **Mesh threshold:** "~4–6 participants for comfort, ~10 is SFU territory" is engineering judgment derived from the cited bandwidth math (N−1 uplinks, five 720p/1.5 Mbps streams as the illustrative ceiling); there is no standards body that publishes a mesh cutoff.

No further follow-up needed unless you want me to dig into a specific SFU's deployment sizing (e.g., mediasoup worker/CPU counts for your expected concurrency).
